name: Pokhara Street Festival
summary: Pokhara's New Year street festival turns about 3.5 km of Lakeside Road into a five-day car-free fair of food stalls, cultural floats, music stages and lake races. Held every year since the late 1990s, it is the biggest street party in western Nepal.
body: The festival is organised by the Pokhara chapter of the Restaurant and Bar Association of Nepal and has run for nearly three decades, normally from 28 December to 1 January. For five days the main Lakeside road is closed to traffic, and restaurants and hotels set up stalls along its length, serving Nepali, Newar, Thakali, Tibetan, Indian and international food. Craft sellers, local producers and sponsors fill the gaps, and the whole strip becomes one long walking street from the morning until late at night.

The opening day usually features a parade of cultural floats and dancers from Nepal's many ethnic communities: Gurung, Magar, Thakali, Newar, Tharu and others in traditional dress. Through the week there are music and dance stages, folk duet performances, art and photo exhibitions, talks on tourism, and lake events such as boat races on Phewa and fun competitions like waiters' races and tug-of-war. The atmosphere is relaxed and family-friendly in the day and lively at night.

The festival builds to the countdown on 31 December, when Lakeside is packed with visitors from across Nepal and India and the party continues past midnight. Hotel prices rise and rooms sell out for the last nights of December, so book early. Exact dates and programmes are announced each year by the organisers, so check current status before you travel. Nearby streets are also busy, so allow extra time for transfers.
tips: Book Lakeside hotels at least two months ahead for 30 and 31 December, when rooms sell out.
Walk the festival in the late afternoon for food and floats, and return after dark for music.
Keep valuables secure and agree a meeting point with children, as crowds are very dense on New Year's Eve.

faqs.a: It is usually held from 28 December to 1 January every year along Lakeside Road beside Phewa Lake, ending with New Year celebrations. Dates and the programme are confirmed each year by the organisers, the Pokhara chapter of the Restaurant and Bar Association of Nepal, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Pokhara Street Festival good for families?
faqs.a: Yes, during the day and early evening. Food stalls, cultural floats, dance stages and lake events are fun for all ages, and the road is closed to traffic. Late nights, especially 31 December, get very crowded and noisy, so families with small children may prefer to watch from a hotel terrace.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for Pokhara Street Festival?
faqs.a: No. The festival is free to enter and spread along about 3.5 km of public road at Lakeside. You pay only for food, drinks and anything you buy at the stalls. Some special events or concerts at private venues may charge separately.

faqs.q: Do hotel prices rise during Pokhara Street Festival?
faqs.a: Yes. Lakeside hotels are in high demand from about 28 December, and the last two nights of the year often sell out with higher rates and minimum-stay rules. Our New Year packages need early booking. Damside and Pardi hotels can be easier to find at short notice.

name: Teej in Pokhara
image_query: Teej women red saris Nepal temple
summary: Haritalika Teej is the women's festival of late summer, when Hindu women dress in red, fast for their husbands' long life or a good marriage, and sing and dance at temples. In Pokhara the crowds gather at Tal Barahi on Phewa Lake and at Bindhyabasini.
body: Teej falls in the Nepali month of Bhadra, usually between mid-August and mid-September, and is dedicated to the goddess Parvati, who according to legend fasted and prayed until Shiva accepted her as his wife. Married women fast for the health and long life of their husbands, and unmarried women for a good husband. Many keep a strict fast without even water on the main day, after a feast called dar khane the night before, when families and friends gather to eat, sing and dance.

On the main day, Pokhara fills with women in red and green saris, red bangles, glass beads and gold jewellery. Lines of devotees form at the boat ghats to cross to Tal Barahi temple on Phewa Lake, and at Bindhyabasini temple above the Old Bazaar, where women offer flowers, fruit and lamps. In temple courtyards and along Lakeside, groups sing Teej songs, some devotional, some light-hearted and some sharply critical of social issues, and dance in circles for hours.

Teej falls in the monsoon, so expect rain, cloud and fewer foreign visitors, which makes it a good time to see local life rather than mountain views. Visitors are welcome to watch and photograph from a respectful distance; ask before photographing individuals. Dates follow the lunar calendar and change every year, so check current dates before you travel. Hotel rates in Pokhara are lower in this season, and the green rice terraces around the valley make the wet weather easier to accept.
tips: Arrive at the Barahi ghat early in the morning, as queues for boats to Tal Barahi grow long by mid-morning.
Carry an umbrella or rain jacket, since Teej falls in the monsoon and showers are frequent.
Ask before photographing women at prayer or dancing, and avoid using flash inside temples.

faqs.a: Teej falls in the Nepali month of Bhadra, usually between mid-August and mid-September, on dates set by the lunar calendar. The exact day is announced each year by Nepal's calendar committee and is a public holiday for women. Check current dates before you travel and plan Pokhara visits around the main day.

faqs.q: Where can I see Teej celebrations in Pokhara?
faqs.a: The biggest gatherings are at Tal Barahi temple on its island in Phewa Lake, reached by boat from Lakeside, and at Bindhyabasini temple above the Old Bazaar. Groups also sing and dance along Lakeside and in community halls. Mornings are busiest at the temples.

Visitors are welcome to watch and often to join the dancing when invited, especially women. Dress modestly, remove shoes at temples and ask before taking close-up photos. Do not eat in front of fasting women in temple areas. Many women enjoy explaining the festival to curious visitors.

faqs.q: Is August a good time to visit Pokhara for Teej?
faqs.a: It is good for culture but not for mountain views. August is the heart of the monsoon in Pokhara, with heavy rain, cloud hiding the peaks and some adventure activities limited. In return you see a major festival, green rice terraces and fewer tourists, with lower hotel prices.
